4th Grade PE · Unit 1.1 · Intro to P.E.
Week 1

Your Body Is Built to Move

Whether you're sprinting across the playground, dancing in the living room, or biking around the block, your body is doing something incredible. This week, you'll learn what actually happens inside you when you move — and why physical education matters for every single person, not just star athletes.

1
Lesson 1
What Counts as Physical Activity?

Physical activity is any movement that makes your body work and use energy. That covers a lot of ground — way more than just sports. Running, climbing, dancing, biking, hiking, swimming, even raking leaves all count.

Here's something important: PE isn't only for kids who love sports or want to be professional athletes. Every body needs movement to stay healthy and strong. Doctors, scientists, teachers, video game designers — everyone needs to move their body almost every day. Your goal isn't to be the fastest or the strongest. It's to keep moving in ways that feel good to you.

2
Lesson 2
What Happens Inside When You Move

When you run, jump, or stretch, your body shifts into a totally different mode. Let's break down what's happening under the surface.

❤️
Heart
It's a muscle, and exercise makes it stronger. A stronger heart pumps more blood with less effort.
🫁
Lungs
They become more efficient, pulling in extra oxygen so your muscles have the fuel they need.
💪
Muscles
Tiny fibers rebuild themselves a little tougher every time you use them.
🦴
Bones
Weight-bearing activity (like running or jumping) signals bones to grow denser and stronger.
🧠
Brain
More blood flow means sharper focus and better memory at school.
💡Did You Know?

Your heart beats around 100,000 times every day — even while you sleep. During hard exercise, it can speed up to nearly double that rate to push extra oxygen out to your working muscles. Over a lifetime, that's about 2.5 billion heartbeats. Treating your heart well now pays off for decades.

3
Lesson 3
Movement Changes How You Feel

Physical activity doesn't just change your body — it also changes your mood and how your brain works. When you exercise, your brain releases chemicals called endorphins — natural mood boosters that can leave you feeling calmer and happier for hours after a workout.

Regular movement helps you:

  • Feel happier — those endorphins act like a natural mood lifter.
  • Handle stress better — exercise burns off the tension that builds up during a tough day.
  • Focus more easily — active kids often find it easier to pay attention in class.
  • Sleep deeper — your body uses sleep to repair and grow after exercise.
🌎Real-World Connection

Professional athletes like Serena Williams, LeBron James, and Simone Biles all talk about how movement helps their mental game just as much as their physical performance. Even on rest days, they walk, stretch, or do light yoga — because they know movement keeps their minds sharp and their stress low.

4
Lesson 4
PE Builds More Than Muscles

Physical education classrooms (and playgrounds) are also where you build sportsmanship — the habit of being respectful, fair, and supportive whether you're winning or losing. When you play games with classmates, you practice:

  • Teamwork — figuring out how to coordinate with people who have different strengths.
  • Following rules — making sure the game stays fair for everyone.
  • Encouraging others — cheering for a teammate who's struggling or congratulating someone who beat you.
  • Handling losses — staying positive when things don't go your way.

These skills carry over into everything — group projects, family life, future jobs.

💭Think About It

Imagine your favorite athlete after losing a big game. How do you think they handle it? What habits do you think they practice to stay positive and try again? Those same habits work for you too.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
  • Physical Activity — Any movement that uses energy, from playing tag to walking the dog.
  • Heart — The muscle that pumps blood (and oxygen) through your entire body.
  • Muscles — Tissues that contract and relax to make your body move.
  • Sportsmanship — Treating teammates and opponents with fairness and respect.
  • Endurance — How long your body can keep moving before it gets tired.
  • Teamwork — Working together with others toward a shared goal.
📝Weekly Reflection

This Week's Reflection: Compare a day when you moved a lot (recess, sports, dancing) with a day when you sat for most of it (long car ride, sick day). How did you feel differently in your body, your mood, and your focus? What patterns do you notice?

→What's Next

Up next: Week 1 VR Assignment — Fitness Park. You'll explore a virtual fitness park and try out activities that get every part of your body moving.

Flight Club

Welcome to Flight Club! 🦊

Flight Club is the optional weekly challenge that runs all year long in 4th-grade PE. It's where you push yourself a little further, earn points, climb the owl ranks, and build movement habits that stick. Read this guide carefully — it explains exactly how the whole thing works.

1
Lesson 1
How It Works

Every unit in this course comes with its own Flight Club challenge. Each challenge contains two or three movements — usually a mix of strength, balance, flexibility, or rhythm moves connected to that unit's theme.

Your job is simple:

  1. Watch the challenge video to learn the movements.
  2. Practice the moves at home or during recess.
  3. Submit a short video or photo showing yourself doing each movement.
  4. Earn points and climb the owl ranks.

You can submit anytime during the unit. Late is okay — but on-time submissions unlock bonus points (more on that below).

2
Lesson 2
Ranking System

Every Flight Club member earns points throughout the year. Your total points place you in one of five Rank tiers:

🦅
Soaring Owl
85–100 points
🦉
Wise Owl
70–84 points
🌫
Gliding Owl
50–69 points
🦊
Fluttering Owl
30–49 points
🧇
Nestling Learner
0–29 points

Every rank is something to be proud of — they all represent progress. The higher tiers just take more consistency to reach.

3
Lesson 3
How to Earn Points

Points stack up across the year, so even small efforts add up. Here's how you score:

  • 5 points for every stretch or movement you complete and submit.
  • 10 bonus points for every perfect month — meaning every Flight Club challenge that month was submitted on time.
  • Year-end rank adds to your overall PE grade. The higher your owl rank, the bigger the boost.

That means a single challenge with three movements is worth 15 points before any bonus. Stack up a perfect month and you've added another 10. Stay steady and the Streak keeps growing.

🌎Real-World Connection

NBA players, professional dancers, and Olympic athletes don't get amazing at their craft overnight — they practice the same movements every single day, sometimes for years. A pro basketball player might shoot 500 free throws a day. A ballet dancer rehearses the same footwork hundreds of times. Flight Club uses the same principle on a kid-sized scale: small, repeated practice turns into real improvement.

4
Lesson 4
Tips to Climb the Ranks

Want to push toward Soaring Owl? Use these strategies:

  • Set a weekly reminder to check for the new Flight Club Challenge.
  • Practice each movement two or three times before recording, so you nail your best take.
  • Submit early — never wait until the last day. Tech problems happen.
  • Treat your monthly streak like a game: keep it alive!
  • Use the reflection prompts to spot which movements you've mastered and which still need work.
5
Lesson 5
Vocabulary

Flight Club Vocabulary

  • Flight Club — The year-long optional challenge program in 4th-grade PE.
  • Challenge — A short set of two or three movements tied to a unit.
  • Points — Earned for each movement completed and submitted.
  • Rank — Your owl tier, based on total points earned.
  • Streak — A run of consecutive on-time submissions.
  • Reflection — Thinking about what you learned and how you improved.
→What's Next

Ready to start? Head to your first Flight Club challenge in Unit 1 and submit your video. Every great Soaring Owl started with a single takeoff.

4th Grade PE · Unit 1.2 · Warm-Ups & Cool-Downs
Week 3

Warm-Ups and Cool-Downs: How Smart Athletes Train

Think about a car on a cold morning. You wouldn't slam the gas pedal the second you turn the key — the engine needs a minute to warm up. Your body works the same way. Before exercise, you warm up. After exercise, you cool down. These two routines are what separate athletes who stay healthy from athletes who get injured.

1
Lesson 1
What a Warm-Up Actually Does

A warm-up is a short routine of light movement (usually 5 to 10 minutes) that prepares your body for harder exercise. It might seem like extra work, but skipping it is one of the fastest ways to get hurt.

A good warm-up gives you four big benefits:

  • Flexible muscles. Warm muscles stretch farther without tearing. Cold muscles snap like dry rubber bands.
  • Ready heart. Your heart rate climbs gradually instead of jumping all at once, which is safer and feels better.
  • Mental focus. Those few minutes help your brain switch from "school mode" to "let's move" mode.
  • Injury prevention. Warm joints and muscles handle sudden movement without strain.
2
Lesson 2
Why You Can't Skip the Cool-Down

A cool-down is the opposite of a warm-up — gentle movement and stretching AFTER exercise to ease your body back to a resting state.

When you stop hard exercise suddenly, blood can pool in your legs and arms, sometimes making you feel dizzy or shaky. Cool-downs prevent that and give your body a head start on recovery — the process of repairing and refueling so you feel ready to go again tomorrow.

❤️‍🩹
Heart Rate Drops
Your heart slows down safely instead of crashing.
🧘
Muscles Stretch
Stretching warm muscles improves flexibility long-term.
🩸
Blood Returns
Blood flows back to your heart and brain properly.
💤
Less Soreness
You wake up feeling better the next day.
💡Did You Know?

Sports scientists studied thousands of athletes and found that those who warmed up and cooled down properly were significantly less likely to suffer injury — damage to muscles, tendons, or joints — compared to those who skipped these routines. It's not magic; it's basic body science.

3
Try It
A 5-Move Warm-Up Routine

Here's a routine you can do anywhere in about 5 minutes:

💪
Arm Circles
10 forward, 10 backward. Loosens shoulders.
🦘
High Knees
March in place 30 seconds, knees up to waist height.
🔄
Shoulder Rolls
5 forward, 5 backward. Stay loose.
🦶
Toe Touches
Slow reaches down — don't bounce. Hold each for 5 seconds.
🏃
Jog in Place
30 seconds of easy jogging. You should feel slightly out of breath when finished.
✅Check for Understanding

How do you know you're warmed up? Your heart should be beating a little faster, you should feel slightly warm (maybe a tiny bit sweaty), and your joints should feel loose. If you still feel stiff, do one more round.

4
Try It
A 5-Move Cool-Down Routine

After hard exercise, spend at least 5 minutes on these:

🤗
Hug Yourself
Wrap arms across chest, hold 15 seconds each side. Stretches shoulders.
🦋
Butterfly Stretch
Sit with feet pressed together. Gently press knees toward floor.
🌬️
Deep Breathing
Inhale through nose for 4 counts, exhale through mouth for 6 counts.
🌟
Reach for the Sky
Stretch arms overhead, then slowly lower. Repeat 5 times.
🦵
Seated Leg Stretch
Sit with legs straight, reach gently toward toes. Hold 20 seconds.
🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic athletes, NFL players, professional dancers — every elite performer warms up and cools down. Watch a soccer player before a match: they jog, stretch, do drills. Watch them after: they walk it off, stretch, then ice anything sore. Their bodies are their careers, and they treat them that way.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
  • Warm-Up — Light movement that prepares your body for harder exercise.
  • Cool-Down — Gentle movement after exercise that helps your body recover.
  • Stretch — Slowly lengthening a muscle to improve flexibility.
  • Injury — Damage to a muscle, joint, or bone, often from sudden or unprepared movement.
  • Heart Rate — How many times your heart beats per minute.
  • Recovery — The process your body uses to repair and refuel after activity.
📝Weekly Reflection

This Week's Reflection: Predict what would happen if you sprinted hard for 5 minutes without warming up. Which parts of your body would feel it the most, and why? Now predict what would happen if you collapsed onto a couch right after sprinting instead of cooling down. What's the difference?

→What's Next

Up next: Week 3 VR Assignment — Warm-Up Routine. You'll build and run your own warm-up sequence in a virtual gym.

4th Grade PE · Unit 1.3 · Muscular Strength & Endurance
Week 5

Muscular Strength: The Foundation Behind Every Move

When people hear "strength," they often picture bodybuilders lifting giant weights. But real strength is much simpler — and much more useful. It's your body's ability to push, lift, pull, and hold without tiring out. And every kid (yes, including you) is building it every single day.

1
Lesson 1
What Strength Really Means

Strength is the amount of force your muscles can produce. Strong muscles let you move, lift, and support your own body without getting tired quickly.

Here's a common myth: strength means having huge, bulging muscles. That's not true. A gymnast, a rock climber, and a soccer player are all incredibly strong, but they look completely different. Strength shows up as:

  • Power when you sprint or jump
  • Stability when you balance on one foot
  • Endurance when you carry something heavy for a long time
  • Control when you slow down or change direction quickly
2
Lesson 2
Why Strength Matters in Daily Life

You don't need to be a competitive athlete to benefit from strength. Look at how often you use it:

🎒
Carrying Your Backpack
Your shoulders, back, and core all work together.
🧗
Climbing Stairs
Leg muscles push you up; core muscles keep you balanced.
🪑
Good Posture
Strong back muscles keep you sitting up straight without strain.
🛡️
Joint Safety
Strong muscles protect your knees, ankles, and elbows when you fall or twist.
💡Did You Know?

Your body has more than 600 different muscles, and they make up about 40% of your total body weight. Some are tiny — like the muscles that move your eyeballs — and some are huge, like the gluteus maximus in your hips, which is the largest muscle in the human body.

3
Lesson 3
How You Actually Build Strength

The cool thing about building strength is that you don't need a gym or any equipment. Your own body weight provides plenty of resistance. The key idea: muscles get stronger when you challenge them, then let them rest and rebuild.

🙌
Push-Ups
Arms, shoulders, chest, and core all work together.
🦵
Squats
The most useful exercise for legs and hips.
🪵
Planks
Build your core — the muscles around your middle that keep you stable.
🐒
Playground Bars
Hanging and climbing build grip and upper-body strength.
🧹
Chores
Carrying laundry, sweeping, helping with groceries — all real strength training.
🏃Activity Cue

Try this right now: Stand up, sit back down, stand up, sit back down — 10 times in a row, no hands. Congratulations — you just did 10 bodyweight squats. Notice how your thighs feel? That's the muscle responding to the challenge.

🌎Real-World Connection

NBA basketball player Stephen Curry isn't the tallest or heaviest player in the league, but his trainers say his core and leg strength are part of why he can shoot accurately even when defenders push him. Strength isn't about size — it's about how your muscles work together. The same is true for dancers, surfers, and martial artists.

4
Lesson 4
Strong Body, Confident Mind

Strong muscles change more than just what you can lift. They change how you feel about yourself.

When you can do something today that you couldn't do last month — one more push-up, a longer plank, climbing higher on the bars — you build endurance along with confidence. You learn that hard work pays off, that your body responds when you put in the effort, and that small improvements add up over time.

Strong people also get injured less often. Strong muscles act like cushions around your joints, absorbing impacts when you jump, land, or change direction. Strength isn't optional for athletes — it's protective for every single body.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
  • Strength — The amount of force your muscles can produce.
  • Muscles — Tissues that contract to create movement and support your body.
  • Exercise — Planned movement designed to improve fitness.
  • Posture — How you hold your body when sitting, standing, or moving.
  • Endurance — How long a muscle can work before it gets tired.
  • Core — The muscles around your stomach and back that stabilize your whole body.
📝Weekly Reflection

This Week's Reflection: Think about your strongest body part (maybe your legs, your arms, your core) and your weakest. Why might that difference exist? What activities have you done a lot of, and what have you done less? How could you train the weaker area to catch up?

→What's Next

Up next: Week 5 VR — Strength Map. You'll explore which exercises build which muscles and create your own strength training map.

pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online

4th Grade PE · Unit 1.4 · Cardiovascular Fitness
Week 7

Cardiovascular Fitness: Your Heart's Workout

Your heart and lungs are a team. They work together every second of every day, but when you exercise, they really shine. "Cardio" exercise is anything that gets your heart pumping fast and your lungs working harder. The better your cardiovascular system gets, the more energy you have for everything else in life.

1
Lesson 1
What 'Cardio' Actually Means

The word cardiovascular comes from two Latin words: cardio means heart, and vascular means blood vessels. So cardiovascular fitness is a measure of how well your heart and blood vessels work together to deliver oxygen to your muscles.

Cardio exercise is any sustained activity that keeps your heart rate elevated. That includes:

  • Running, jogging, sprinting
  • Jumping rope or doing jumping jacks
  • Dancing for more than a few minutes
  • Biking, swimming, hiking
  • Most team sports — soccer, basketball, hockey

If you're breathing harder than usual and your heart is beating faster, you're doing cardio.

2
Lesson 2
What's Happening Inside During Cardio

When you exercise hard for more than a few minutes, your body kicks into a totally different gear.

❤️
Heart Gets Stronger
It's a muscle — and like any muscle, it grows tougher with use.
🫁
Lungs Pull More Oxygen
Each breath delivers more oxygen to your bloodstream.
🩸
Blood Carries Fuel
Oxygen-rich blood travels to working muscles faster.
🔋
Endurance Climbs
Over weeks, you can exercise longer before you tire.
🧠
Brain Sharpens
More oxygen to your brain means better thinking and memory.
💡Did You Know?

Your blood travels about 12,000 miles through your body each day — that's roughly the distance from New York to Tokyo and back. During hard cardio, your heart can pump four to five times the normal amount of blood per minute to keep up with your muscles' demand for oxygen.

3
Lesson 3
How Cardio Affects Your Mood and Brain

Cardio doesn't just train your heart — it transforms your mental state. Studies show that regular cardio activity helps kids and adults:

  • Feel energized instead of sluggish, especially during the school day.
  • Release happy chemicals (endorphins) that lift your mood for hours afterward.
  • Focus longer on reading, homework, and tasks that require concentration.
  • Sleep more deeply at night, which means waking up feeling refreshed.
  • Handle stress better when school or family life gets challenging.
🌎Real-World Connection

Many schools have started "movement breaks" between classes — 5 minutes of jumping jacks, running in place, or dancing. Research shows that students who take these breaks score higher on tests and pay attention longer than students who sit still all day. Your body and brain literally work better when you move them.

4
Lesson 4
Cardio That Doesn't Feel Like Exercise

Cardio doesn't have to mean running boring laps. The best cardio is the kind you actually enjoy enough to keep doing.

🎮
Tag Games
Freeze tag, sharks and minnows — sprint, change directions, repeat.
💃
Dancing
Crank a playlist and move for 15 minutes. That's a workout.
🏀
Pickup Sports
Basketball, soccer, four-square with friends or family.
🪢
Jump Rope
Just 10 minutes equals a serious cardio session.
🚴
Bike Rides
Around the block, to a friend's house, on a trail.
🏃Activity Cue

Try this: Set a timer for 60 seconds and do jumping jacks the whole time. Then put your hand on your chest. You should feel your heart pounding noticeably faster than normal. That's your cardiovascular system responding to the challenge.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
  • Cardiovascular — Relating to your heart and blood vessels working together.
  • Heart Rate — How many times your heart beats per minute.
  • Endurance — How long your body can keep moving before it tires.
  • Oxygen — The gas your body needs to convert food into usable energy.
  • Cardio Exercise — Sustained activity that raises your heart rate.
  • Fitness — Your overall ability to perform physical activities efficiently.
📝Weekly Reflection

This Week's Reflection: Compare how you feel after 30 seconds of jumping jacks with how you feel after sitting still for 30 minutes. What changed inside your body? Think about your heart rate, your breathing, your energy, and your mood. Why does movement create such a big shift?

→What's Next

Up next: Week 7 VR — Build Your Own Track. You'll design a custom cardio route and explore how different paces affect your heart and energy.

pages.title: Week 9: Flexibility & Stretching
pages.html:
Optima
Academy Online
Mission: Move!
4th Grade PE · Unit 1.5 · Flexibility & Stretching
Week 9

Flexibility and Stretching: The Hidden Superpower

Flexibility is one of those fitness skills that doesn't get a lot of attention — until you don't have it. Tight muscles make every other activity harder and increase your chance of getting hurt. The good news? Flexibility is something every body can improve, no matter where you're starting.

1
Lesson 1
What Flexibility Actually Is

Flexibility is your body's ability to bend, twist, reach, and stretch through a full range of motion without pain or stiffness. It's measured by how far your joints — the places where two bones meet, like your knees, elbows, hips, and shoulders — can move comfortably.

Flexibility isn't the same for every part of your body. You might have super-flexible hips but tight shoulders, or loose ankles but a stiff back. That's totally normal — and it's why a well-rounded stretching routine pays attention to every major area.

2
Lesson 2
What Happens When You Stretch

Stretching is the practice of slowly lengthening a muscle and holding it. When you stretch correctly, your muscle fibers gradually lengthen and relax, which produces a long list of benefits.

🌡️
Warms the Muscle
Blood flow increases, making the muscle more pliable.
🛡️
Prevents Injury
Flexible muscles tear less easily during sudden movements.
🧘
Releases Tension
Tight muscles often hold stress — stretching lets it go.
⚖️
Improves Balance
Flexible hips and ankles help you stay steady.
😌
Feels Great
A good stretch is genuinely one of the best feelings.
💡Did You Know?

Your body is most flexible after exercise, when your muscles are already warm. Stretching cold muscles (right when you wake up, for example) can actually cause small tears. That's why the smartest order is: light movement first, then stretch — and definitely stretch after exercise when your muscles are warm and pliable.

3
Lesson 3
How Flexibility Changes How You Feel

Beyond the physical benefits, regular stretching changes how you feel mentally too:

  • Relaxed — your body feels lighter, less tense.
  • Less stiff — especially helpful after a long day of school or screen time.
  • More aware — you start noticing which areas hold tension and can address them.
  • Proud — improvements in flexibility happen quickly, which feels rewarding.

Many people use stretching as a calm-down routine before bed because it slows down both the body and the mind.

🌎Real-World Connection

Olympic gymnasts, ballerinas, and martial artists spend a huge portion of their training on flexibility. But it's not just athletes — surgeons stretch their hands and wrists before long operations, pianists stretch their fingers, and astronauts on the International Space Station have a full stretching protocol because their bodies stiffen in zero gravity. Flexibility matters in every field.

4
Try It
5 Stretches That Feel Amazing

Add these to your routine after exercise or before bed. Hold each one for 15 to 30 seconds. Breathe slowly — never bounce.

⭐
Reach for the Stars
Stand tall, stretch arms straight up, fingers pointed at the ceiling.
🐈
Cat Stretch
On hands and knees, arch your back like a cat, then drop it down.
🦩
Flamingo Hold
Stand on one foot, hold the other knee to your chest. Switch sides.
🦋
Butterfly
Sit with feet together, gently press knees toward floor.
🌊
Side Reach
Stand tall, reach one arm overhead and lean to the opposite side.
🏃Activity Cue

Try this: Stand up, reach toward the ceiling, and hold for 10 seconds. Now slowly bend forward and reach toward your toes — go only as far as feels good — and hold for 10 seconds. Notice how your back, legs, and shoulders feel different than they did before. That's flexibility in action.

5
Vocabulary
Words to Know
  • Flexibility — How easily your body can bend, twist, and stretch.
  • Stretching — Gently lengthening a muscle and holding it.
  • Joints — Places where two bones meet, like knees, elbows, and shoulders.
  • Balance — Your ability to stay steady while standing, moving, or changing direction.
  • Injury — Damage to a muscle, joint, or bone — often caused by sudden, unprepared movement.
  • Muscles — The tissues that contract to make your body move and stretch.
📝Weekly Reflection

This Week's Reflection: Compare how your body feels first thing in the morning, before you've moved much, versus after 5 minutes of stretching. Why might it feel so different? What's actually changing in your muscles and joints during those 5 minutes?

→What's Next

Up next: Week 9 VR — Flexibility. You'll explore a virtual stretching studio and design a personal flexibility routine that targets your tightest areas.

pages.html:
Optima

4th Grade PE · Unit 1.6 · Nutrition
Week 11

Nutrition: Fueling the Machine That Is You

Your body is one of the most complex machines in the universe, and like any machine, it runs on fuel. The fuel you choose — the food and drinks you put in — directly affects how you feel, how you think, how you grow, and how you perform. Nutrition isn't about being perfect. It's about understanding what's actually happening inside.

1
Lesson 1
What Nutrition Really Is

Nutrition is the study of how your body uses the food and drinks you consume to grow, repair itself, and produce energy — the fuel your body uses for everything from running and thinking to keeping your heart beating.

Every bite of food contains nutrients — substances your body breaks down and uses for different jobs. Some nutrients build muscle. Some power your brain. Some strengthen your bones. Some help you fight off illness. No single food has everything you need, which is why eating a balanced meal — a meal that includes a variety of food groups — is so important.

2
Lesson 2
The Five Food Groups (and Water)

Nutrition experts organize food into five main groups, plus hydration. Each group plays a different role.

🥬
Vegetables
Loaded with vitamins and fiber. Broccoli, spinach, carrots, peppers.
🍎
Fruits
Natural sugars + vitamins. Apples, berries, oranges, bananas.
🌾
Grains
Long-lasting fuel. Bread, rice, pasta, oats — whole grain is best.
🍗
Proteins
Protein builds muscle. Chicken, fish, beans, eggs, nuts.
🥛
Dairy
Calcium for strong bones and teeth. Milk, yogurt, cheese.
💧
Water
Hydration keeps every cell working. Aim for 6–8 cups daily.
💡Did You Know?

Your brain is about 75% water. Even mild dehydration — being just 1 to 2 percent low on water — can make it harder to concentrate, slow down your reaction time, and make you feel tired or grumpy. Most kids don't drink enough water, especially during school. Carrying a water bottle is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

3
Lesson 3
What Healthy Eating Does for Your Body

When your meals include foods from each group, your body gets everything it needs to operate at full power.

  • Sharper brain — protein, healthy fats, and steady carbs power your thinking.
  • Stronger muscles — protein rebuilds the tiny fibers you damage during exercise.
  • Healthier heart — vegetables, fruits, and whole grains keep your blood vessels clear.
  • Energy that lasts — balanced meals release energy slowly, so you don't crash mid-afternoon.
  • Better sleep — what you eat affects how deeply you sleep at night.
  • Fewer sick days — vitamins from real food strengthen your immune system.
🌎Real-World Connection

Compare two snack choices: a candy bar versus an apple with peanut butter. The candy bar gives you a quick sugar spike followed by a crash about 30 minutes later, leaving you tired and hungry again. The apple with peanut butter gives you steady energy for two or three hours because the protein and fiber slow down how fast your body absorbs the sugar. Same number of calories, totally different effect on your day.

4
Lesson 4
Why Nutrition Can Be Fun

Eating well doesn't mean giving up everything delicious. Some of the most enjoyable parts of nutrition are:

  • Trying new foods — every culture has incredible dishes you've never tasted.
  • Cooking — making your own food is a real-life skill that's also creative and fun.
  • Helping at home — meal prep with family is a way to learn AND spend time together.
  • Experimenting — combining flavors, building your own snacks, finding what you love.

Treats are fine too. The goal isn't perfection — it's making most of your meals colorful, varied, and balanced. Pizza and cake are part of life. So are fruits and vegetables. The trick is to keep the balance tipped in favor of foods that fuel you well.

🏃Activity Cue

Challenge: Build a "rainbow plate" this week. Week 13

Locomotor Skills: The Engines That Move You

Every time you change your spot on the planet — walking to class, sprinting after a soccer ball, hopping over a puddle — you're using locomotor skills. They're the building blocks behind almost every sport, game, and dance you'll ever try.

1
Lesson 1
What Does "Locomotor" Even Mean?

The word locomotor comes from locomotive — that giant engine on the front of a train that pulls everything down the track. Your locomotor skills are kind of like that. They're the movements that carry your whole body from one place to another.

Anytime you travel, hop, glide, or zoom across a space, you're using a locomotor skill. The cool part is there are EIGHT of them, and each one trains your body in a slightly different way.

2
Lesson 2
The 8 Basic Locomotor Skills

Let's meet the whole team. These eight movements show up in pretty much every sport and active game on Earth.

🚶
Walking
The first skill you ever learned. Smooth, steady, predictable — one foot always touches the ground.
🏃
Running
Like walking, but faster — and for a split second, both feet leave the ground.
🦘
Jumping
Take off with both feet, land with both feet. Great for power and explosiveness.
🦩
Hopping
Take off and land on the SAME single foot. A real balance challenge.
🎶
Skipping
A step followed by a hop, then switch feet. Rhythm and coordination combined.
🦒
Leaping
A BIG step — push off one foot, land on the other. Used in dance and hurdles.
🐴
Galloping
One foot leads, the other catches up. Same lead foot the whole time.
↔️
Sliding
Sideways movement, like guarding someone in basketball. Stay low, stay quick.
💡Did You Know?

Your brain remembers how to walk so well that it does it without thinking — that's called automatic motor memory. But hopping on one foot uses a different brain pathway, which is why it feels harder. Every time you practice a new locomotor skill, you're actually building fresh wiring inside your brain.

3
Lesson 3
Why These Skills Matter So Much

Here's the secret PE teachers love sharing: master the eight locomotor skills, and you've already won half the battle in sports. Soccer? You're running, sliding, and leaping. Basketball? Running, jumping, sliding. Tag? Every single one.

Beyond sports, locomotor practice builds four powerful body systems:

  • Balance — staying steady, especially in hopping and skipping
  • Coordination — getting your brain, arms, and legs to cooperate
  • Spatial awareness — knowing exactly where your body is so you don't crash into people or furniture
  • Agility — changing direction quickly without falling or losing speed
🌎Real-World Connection

Astronauts returning from months in space have to RELEARN how to walk because their brains adjusted to zero gravity. Coaches and physical therapists guide them through basic locomotor drills — walking, then skipping, then galloping — to rebuild that brain-to-body connection. The same skills you practice in PE are what doctors use to retrain Olympic-level humans.

4
Try It
The Locomotor Challenge

Pick a safe, open space at home — a hallway, your bedroom, or the yard. Try traveling across it five different ways, in order:

  1. Walk across normally
  2. Hop across on your LEFT foot only
  3. Skip across (step-hop, step-hop)
  4. Gallop with your right foot leading
  5. Slide sideways, low and quick

Pay attention to which one feels smoothest and which one feels trickiest. That's useful information about your body!

5
Lesson 5
Words to Know

Your Movement Vocabulary

  • Locomotor — Any movement that travels your body from place to place.
  • Balance — Keeping your body steady while still or moving.
  • Coordination — When your brain and different body parts work together smoothly.
  • Spatial Awareness — Knowing where your body is in space compared to people and objects.
  • Agility — The ability to change direction quickly with control.
  • Hop — A jump on one foot, landing on the same foot.
  • Gallop — A travel pattern where one foot leads and the other follows.
📝Weekly Reflection

Compare hopping on one foot vs. galloping. Which one is harder for you, and why might that be? Think about which body parts each skill uses and how balance plays a role in each.

→What's Next

Week 15

Throwing & Catching: The Art of Aim and Snag

Anytime you control an object with your body — a ball, a frisbee, a beanbag — you're using manipulative skills. Throwing and catching are two of the most important ones, and they show up in almost every sport you can think of.

1
Lesson 1
What Are Manipulative Skills?

Manipulative skills are movements where your body controls an object. The word manipulate just means "to handle or control." So whenever you toss, catch, kick, dribble, or strike something, you're manipulating it.

Today we're zooming in on two of the biggest:

  • Throwing — using your arm and body to send an object toward a target
  • Catching — using your hands and eyes to receive an object coming at you

These two skills are partners. Almost every sport that involves a ball uses both.

2
Lesson 2
The Mechanics of a Good Throw

A great throw isn't just about a strong arm. Your whole body works together like a chain of energy — feet, hips, core, shoulder, arm, and finally the hand release.

👀
Eyes
Lock onto the target before you throw. Where your eyes go, the ball follows.
🦶
Feet
Step toward the target with your OPPOSITE foot from your throwing arm.
🌀
Hips
Twist your hips toward the target — this is where most of your power comes from.
💪
Arm
Pull back, then snap forward in a smooth arc. Follow through past your target.
3
Lesson 3
The Mechanics of a Good Catch

Catching looks simple — but a good catch uses a surprising amount of brain work. Your eyes have to track a moving object, your brain has to predict where it will arrive, and your hands have to be in the right place at the right millisecond.

The key to catching is hand-eye coordination — your eyes and hands working together as a team. Strong catchers do four things:

  • Watch the object all the way into their hands
  • Move their body to get in front of it
  • Reach out with both hands, fingers spread and relaxed
  • "Give" with the catch — pull the object softly toward their body
💡Did You Know?

The average Major League Baseball pitcher throws around 90 miles per hour, and the batter only has about 0.4 seconds to decide whether to swing. That's why pro athletes train their hand-eye coordination with reaction drills — the better your brain processes moving objects, the better your timing becomes in every sport.

4
Lesson 4
Why These Skills Are Worth Practicing

Throwing and catching show up everywhere: baseball, basketball, football, frisbee, lacrosse, water polo, dodgeball, cricket. But the benefits go way beyond sports.

🎯
Accuracy
Aiming a throw teaches your brain to control fine details of movement.
💪
Upper Body Strength
Throwing builds shoulders, arms, and especially your core.
⏱️
Timing
Catching trains you to predict when and where something will arrive.
🤝
Teamwork
A throw is incomplete without someone to catch it. You learn to communicate.
🌎Real-World Connection

Quarterbacks in the NFL spend more practice time on accuracy drills than almost anything else. They throw at moving targets, into wind, behind their backs — all to train their bodies to repeat the same motion under pressure. That same kind of practice (just at YOUR level) is what helps a beanbag toss become a strike from the outfield someday.

5
Lesson 5
Words to Know

Your Throwing & Catching Vocabulary

  • Manipulative Skills — Movements where your body controls an object.
  • Throw — Using your arm and body to send an object through the air.
  • Catch — Using your hands to receive a moving object safely.
  • Hand-Eye Coordination — Your eyes and hands working together as a team.
  • Accuracy — How close you get to your target.
  • Control — Handling an object the way you want, not by accident.
📝Weekly Reflection

Predict what would happen if you tried to catch a ball with your eyes closed. Why? Use what you learned about hand-eye coordination to explain your prediction.

Toe Touch Stretch (Waterfall Stretch)

How to do it:

  • Stand up tall with feet together.
  • Slowly bend forward and reach for your toes, keeping legs straight.
  • Let your arms "flow down" like a waterfall.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then slowly stand up.

Benefits: Stretches hamstrings (back of the thighs) and lower back.

2
Butterfly Stretch

How to do it:

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.
  • Keep your back straight and hold the stretch.
  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Benefits: Stretches the inner thighs and hips.

3
Flamingo Stretch (Quadriceps Stretch)

How to do it:

  • Stand tall and bend one knee, bringing your foot behind you.
  • Hold your ankle with your hand and keep your balance.
  • Keep your knees close together and hold for 10 seconds.
  • Switch legs and repeat.
  • Optional: Extend one arm forward like a flamingo's neck!

Benefits: Stretches the front of the thigh (quadriceps) and improves balance.

Side Lunge Stretch (Skater Stretch)

How to do it:

  • Stand with feet wide apart.
  • Bend one knee and shift your weight to that side, keeping the other leg straight.
  • Hold for 10 seconds, then switch sides.
  • Optional: Pretend you're an ice skater gliding side to side!

Forearm Plank

How to do it:

  • Get into a plank position with arms straight and back flat.
  • Hold for 30 seconds without dropping your belly.
  • Challenge: Try tapping one shoulder at a time while holding the plank.
  • Modification: Try a knee plank if needed.

Benefits: Builds core and upper body strength.

3
Push Ups

How to do it:

  • Start by lying on your stomach with your hands flat on the floor next to your shoulders.
  • Push your body up so your arms are straight and only your hands and toes are touching the ground.
  • Keep your body in a straight line—don't let your back sag or your hips rise.
  • Bend your elbows and lower your body until your chest is close to the floor, then push back up.
  • Try 5 push-ups to start.

Benefits: Builds upper body strength.

How to do it:

  • Stand up tall with feet together.
  • Slowly bend forward and reach for your toes, keeping legs straight.

  • Hold for 10 seconds, then slowly stand up.

Week 12 Flight Club: Balance & Stretch 🦋

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Three challenges that mix balance and flexibility. Focus on staying steady and breathing through each move — that's where the real progress happens.

1
Flamingo Balance

How to do it:

  1. Stand up tall with your feet together.
  2. Gently lift one foot and bend your knee so your foot is behind you.
  3. Hold your arms out to the side like wings for balance.
  4. Try to stay still like a flamingo for 10 seconds.
  5. Switch legs and repeat.

Optional: Try closing one eye or flapping your "wings" for a fun challenge!

Benefits: Builds focus and body control, helping you stay calm and centered.

2
Butterfly Stretch

How to do it:

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.
  • Keep your back straight and hold the stretch.
  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Benefits: Stretches the inner thighs and hips.

3
Arm Circles

How to do it:

  1. Stand up straight with your arms stretched out to the sides, like a big "T."
  2. Slowly make small forward circles with your arms for 10 seconds.
  3. Then, switch directions and make small backward circles for 10 seconds.
  4. Want a challenge? Try making the circles bigger each time!

Optional: Pretend you're flying like a superhero or spinning like a windmill!

Benefits: Warms up your shoulder and arm muscles to get ready for movement.

Week 14 Flight Club: Power Moves 🦸

🚀 Flight Club Challenge

Three power moves to build real strength. Work slow and controlled — that's where muscles grow. Form over speed, every time.

1
Split Squat

How to do it:

  1. Stand up tall with one foot in front and the other foot behind you—like you're about to take a big step.
  2. Keep your front knee over your ankle and your back heel lifted off the ground.
  3. Slowly bend both knees to lower your body straight down.
  4. Stop when your back knee is close to the ground (but not touching!).
  5. Stand back up. Do 5 slow squats, then switch legs and repeat.

Benefits: Makes your leg muscles stronger, especially your thighs and calves.

2
Superman Hold

How to do it:

  1. Lie flat on your stomach on the floor or a soft mat.
  2. Stretch your arms straight out in front of you and your legs straight behind you.
  3. At the same time, lift your arms, chest, and legs slightly off the ground.
  4. Try to hold this pose for 10 seconds—like you're flying through the sky!
  5. Slowly lower back down and rest. Try it again 2–3 more times!

Benefits: Strengthens your back and core muscles.

3
Bench Dips

How to do it:

  1. Find a sturdy chair, bench, or low table. Sit on the edge with your hands next to your hips.
  2. Walk your feet forward and slide your bottom off the edge, so your hands are holding you up.
  3. Bend your elbows to lower your body a little—like you're going down slowly.
  4. Push back up until your arms are straight again.
  5. Try doing 5–10 dips, then take a break!

Benefits: Strengthens your arms, shoulders, and chest.

🏃Activity Cue

A mix of flexibility and strength this week — Butterfly, Plank, and Seated Forward. These three together hit the hips, core, and hamstrings.

1
Butterfly Stretch

How to do it:

  • Sit on the floor with feet together and knees bent outward.
  • Hold your feet with your hands and gently push your knees toward the floor.
  • Keep your back straight and hold the stretch.
  • Optional: Pretend your legs are butterfly wings and gently flap them!

Benefits: Stretches the inner thighs and hips.

2
Forearm Plank

How to do it:

  • Get into a plank position with arms straight and back flat.
  • Hold for 30 seconds without dropping your belly.
  • Challenge: Try tapping one shoulder at a time while holding the plank.
  • Modification: Try a knee plank if needed.

Benefits: Builds core and upper body strength.

3
Seated Forward Stretch

How to do it:

  • Sit on the floor with legs straight in front of you.
  • Reach forward toward your toes while keeping your legs straight.
  • Hold the stretch for 10 seconds, then sit up slowly.

Benefits: Stretches hamstrings and lower back.
